line:
I take breakfast with Lady Maren and ask for one thing: let me tell her village the truth about the ford hero myself, in the Heron and Net's common room, at midday. A confession from the storyteller who found the page would sting less than one from an assessor, and it would give me a crowd of honest witnesses at my back before dusk.

In the afternoon I'll scout the ford and its stepping stones, pick a spot where I can speak with Corvin in the open with Hob Crannock and a few villagers within earshot, and ask Lady Maren to lend me two of her men-at-arms to stand quietly in the willows.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren's confession in the Heron and Net went badly (natural 1 Performance); the villagers are split and angry at Lady Maren; Hob Crannock stood and vouched for Elowen's mark, which steadied some. Afternoon scouting (Perception 13): Garrow hidden in the reeds below the weir; Corvin's wagon under a tarp in an alder copse upstream of the ford, driver asleep on the box. Lady Maren lent two men-at-arms (Pike and Dunn) to wait in the willows.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Lady Maren hears you out over porridge, hesitates for the length of one held breath, and agrees. "Better from you than from a stranger with a seal." She also lends you two men-at-arms, Pike and Dunn, who are to wait in the willows and stay out of sight.

Midday in the Heron and Net goes badly. Your Performance check was a natural 1. Your voice cracks on the first line, you lose the thread of the story you rehearsed, and someone at the back laughs. "Another liar from the spur!" a man shouts. Half the room hears "my lady's family cheated us" and the other half hears "my lady's family is shamed". The mood sours fast, and for a moment you think they might throw you out. Then old Hob Crannock gets to his feet, shaky and loud, and swears on Elowen's lamp to what he saw twenty years ago. That steadies some of them. Others leave muttering. The village is split and wary, and Lady Maren will have to live with the aftermath.

In the afternoon you scout the ford. Your Perception check was a 13, and it pays off. A lean shape in a brown coat is crouched in the reeds below the weir, still as a heron. Upstream, in an alder copse, a painted wagon sits under a tarp, with the driver dozing on the box. You find a flat bank by the stepping stones, in the open, where Hob's cottage and a few cottagers' doorways overlook the water.

It's half past four. Dusk is a couple of hours off. The light is going gold on the water.

What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren confessed the ford hero tale's falseness in the Heron and Net. Crowd mixed: Lady Maren stood beside her, the miller's guild-man Dunstan Pike demanded the toll be struck and ferry-dues refunded, others jeered. Settled for now: Maren promised a village moot in a week. Afternoon scouting: two men-at-arms (Alder and Wick) lent to Wren; willows on the east bank give cover; Hob will sit on his step within earshot. A trampled patch in the reeds upstream suggests someone hid there recently (Garrow or the driver).

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Over breakfast Lady Maren hears you out, sets down her cup, and says, "Say it in my name as well as yours." She agrees to everything, including the loan of two men-at-arms, Alder and Wick, who look glad of a task that isn't collecting tolls.

At noon the Heron and Net is packed. Your speech lands with a 11, which is only half enough. You tell them straight: the hero at the ford was a tale sold to the Thistlewoods, and you hold the page that proves it. Lady Maren stands at your shoulder and doesn't flinch. Some listen. A broad miller's man, Dunstan Pike, bangs his mug and demands the toll be struck and twenty years of dues paid back. Others jeer that you're a stranger stirring trouble. It ends in shouting but no blows, and Maren promises a moot in a week to settle it. The room is split, not hostile. Hob Crannock, on a bench by the door, says loudly that he'll swear to Elowen's mark and sit within earshot at dusk.

In the afternoon you walk the ford. Your Perception check was an 11, not quite sharp enough to be sure of anything. The east-bank willows give good cover for Alder and Wick. The stepping stones run about forty paces across, with Hob's green door at the near end. Upstream, the reeds are flattened in a patch the size of a cart-bed. Someone lay there recently, but you can't tell who or whether they're still there.

It's half past four. Dusk is a couple of hours off. You have the ledger, the commission, the pendant, and a village that's still arguing. Your plan is set, and Corvin hasn't shown himself.

What does Wren do until dusk?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren told the Heron and Net's common room the ford hero was a forgery (Performance 7, clumsy: the room turned angry at first, at Wren and the Thistlewoods; Lady Maren's presence and Hob's word calmed it into a sullen, wary hush). Village now knows. Afternoon: Wren scouted the ford and spotted Garrow lying in the reeds on the far bank, upstream of the stepping stones, plus the tail of Corvin's wagon hidden in an alder copse downstream. Lady Maren lent two men-at-arms (Dunstan and Pell) for the willows.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Lady Maren agrees over breakfast, though she goes pale as she does. "Say it plainly, and I'll stand beside you."

At midday the Heron and Net is packed, with fishers, ferrymen and the toll-keeper's cousins. You climb on a bench and tell them. Your Performance check was a 7, and it goes badly at first. Your words come out too clever, and someone shouts that the Thistlewoods have been robbing them for twenty years and now a girl tells them it was all a song. A tankard hits the wall. Then Lady Maren steps forward and says, in her tired, level voice, "It's true. I knew it might be." Old Hob Crannock raps his stick and swears to Elowen's mark. The room doesn't forgive, but it goes quiet and wary, and the toll is now a question rather than a grievance.

In the afternoon you walk the ford. Your Perception check was a 14. You find the stepping stones, a flat gravel bar mid-stream with a leaning alder, and Hob's cottage in earshot of the bank. You also spot a flattened patch in the reeds on the far bank, upstream. A brown sleeve moves in it: Garrow, lying still. And through a screen of alders downstream, the painted tail of Corvin's wagon, hidden. Lady Maren lends you two men-at-arms, Dunstan and Pell, who slip into the willows on your side without a sound.

It's half past four. Dusk comes in a little over two hours. The river is loud and cold, and the sun is lowering behind the weir.

You can use that time to rest, prepare, or arrange your ground. What does Wren do?

input.description: The true hero of Ashby Weir's ford: a ferrywoman who hauled villagers across in a flood generations ago. The village's toll was always a common right, taken for upkeep, which Corvin's forged tale of a Thistlewood ancestor turned into a lordly one. Revealed to Wren by old Nan Wade at the Heron and Net after her speech.
relationships: true origin of the ford tale in [[Ashby Weir]]
forged over by [[Corvin Tallowmere]] for [[House Thistlewood]]

input.add_to_description: Day 5: Nan Wade (very old, Bess Wade's descendant) tells Wren she saw the road-priest with a lamp-staff cross the ford at night twenty years ago heading down to the old weir-mill, and a man with a shuttered lantern following. The priest never crossed back. The weir-mill is now derelict, and is a likely place for Corvin's meeting. Wren's Perception (9) missed Garrow in the willows.

input.add_to_description: Day 5: agreed to Wren's public confession at the Heron and Net at midday; after Wren's speech, publicly agreed the toll returns to the village's common right and apologised. Lent two men-at-arms to hide in the willows by the ford.

entries.text: notebook: updated Lady Maren Thistlewood
time: 10 hours 15 minutes later: Day 5, 5:15 PM

Lady Maren hears your request over porridge, sets down her spoon, and agrees. "I'd sooner be shamed by you than by the Crown."

At midday the Heron and Net is packed, with fishers, weavers and ferrymen shoulder to shoulder and Lady Maren standing stiffly by the door. You climb onto a bench and tell it the way Corvin taught you, with the story first and the truth tucked inside. Your Performance check was a natural 20, and the room goes silent, then loud, then silent again. You tell them the painting's hero never held the ford, that a storyteller sold the tale, and that you are his apprentice and ashamed of it. Lady Maren steps forward, says the toll is the village's common right as it always was, and apologises. Somebody starts to clap, and somebody else is crying.

Afterwards a very old woman, Nan Wade, takes your sleeve. The true hero, she says, was a ferrywoman, Bess Wade, her own forebear, who hauled the village across in a flood. And she has something for you, since you've given the truth back: twenty years ago she saw a road-priest with a lamp-staff cross the ford at night and go down toward the old weir-mill, and a man with a shuttered lantern following her. The priest never crossed back. The mill has been derelict ever since.

The afternoon you spend scouting the ford, the stepping stones, and the willows. Your Perception check was a 9, and you find a good spot, a flat bank in the open with Hob's doorstep forty paces off, but nothing that tells you who is watching you. Two of Lady Maren's men-at-arms settle quietly into the willows, as you asked.

It's a quarter past five on Day 5, and the light is going copper. Dusk is near. Corvin hasn't appeared, and the old mill squats dark downstream of the weir.

What does Wren do?

Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.
